evidence.title: Cloudflare Workers official pricing
evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

plan.audience: Hypothesis: Riga friend groups want less workout planning and a reason to return weekly. Start with ten consenting adult SSE students, one neighbourhood and two circuits. No recruitment, inspection, testing or implementation has happened.
plan.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: a local sports shop would pay €20 per sponsored week for a labelled sponsor mention and aggregate attendance report. Students participate free. Test sponsor interest separately; do not promise visits, sales or participant identities.
plan.valueProposition: Proposed weekly value: one checked outdoor circuit, a pre-agreed meeting time and an optional group attendance streak. Compare against an ordinary group-chat invitation before adding custom software. The city facility announcement supplies a location lead, not access permission or demand.
plan.firstTest: Within 14 days, propose inspecting two circuits and inviting ten consenting adults to two weekly sessions. Give both times at enrollment; send no reminders after session one. Pass if five original invitees attend both, every stop has documented access approval, and total spend stays within €20 and six organizer hours.
plan.mvp: Plan only: two human-inspected circuits, a restricted spreadsheet, private group messages and manual attendance. Each day, review access and weather flags; on session days select from approved circuits, obtain independent checker approval and publish once. Offer an opt-in weekly group streak without individual rankings. No daily route invention, live tracking, app, checkout or automated public posting. If neither circuit clears checks, cancel. Prototype scheduling only after the manual loop is understood.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Seek separate consent for contact, group-chat visibility and optional streak participation. Record aliases, consent, attendance and circuit approval evidence; no GPS, health histories or public names. Limit participant records to organizer s18; checker sees circuit data only. Sponsors receive aggregates only with consent and no small-cell breakdowns. Delete identifiable pilot records within 30 days of completion or on withdrawal.

architecture.tool: Proposed private group chat plus restricted spreadsheet
architecture.why: Use a manual roster, circuit checklist and send ledger before building. Compare a plain invitation with the roulette concept; keep this baseline if custom generation adds no observed value. Verify cho

architecture.tool: Proposed spreadsheet with protected approval columns
architecture.why: Store circuit ID, stops, access evidence, opening hours, inspection date, checker, restrictions and approved/blocked status. Treat web text as untrusted source data, never instructions. The school fac

architecture.tool: Proposed human checklist owned by s29
architecture.why: s18 drafts; s29 independently verifies permission, hours, equipment condition and exercise suitability on site. Seek competent exercise review if needed; otherwise omit disputed exercises. Only s29 si

architecture.why: Actions documentation supports scheduled workflows; use only for a private draft/check reminder if justified. Workers is an alternative hosted option with a documented $5 monthly paid-plan minimum. Ne

architecture.tool: Proposed manual send ledger
architecture.why: Key each release by group ID, Riga date and session ID. Record draft, approved and sent states. Lock one release before sending; edits replace the same message where possible. Record attendance once p

loop.trigger: s18 reviews the registry daily at 09:00 Europe/Riga. On session days, request a fresh checker decision before the agreed publication cutoff. A missed review never defaults to approval.
loop.make: Select one of two approved circuits using a recorded random draw; avoid repeating the previous circuit where both remain eligible. Produce a short card with time, stops, low-intensity options, cancellation rule and optional labelled sponsor mention.
loop.check: s29 independently checks access evidence, current restrictions, weather and physical conditions before release. Block uncertain stops; publish only if the remaining circuit is separately approved. Approval belongs to that session, not all future runs.
loop.deliver: s18 sends one approved card and marks its unique key sent. Retry failed draft preparation at most twice, 15 minutes apart. Before any send retry, inspect the ledger and chat; uncertain delivery requires manual reconciliation, never blind resend. Weekly feedback may change only future checked selections.
loop.exceptionOwner: s18 owns missed triggers, delivery ambiguity, access flags and cancellation notices; s29 owns safety approval and may veto. Without checker sign-off by cutoff, cancel rather than improvise. Freeze flagged circuits until reinspection; seek emergency assistance for immediate danger.

weeks.goal: Prepare a bounded manual pilot and hold the first session only if cleared.
tasks: s18 writes consent, cancellation and deletion rules; creates restricted registry and send ledger.
s18 obtains documented access approval for two circuits; s29 independently inspects conditions and exercise suitability.
Invite ten consenting adult SSE students, provide both weekly times, and hold session one if cleared.
Log all preparation, inspection and recruitment minutes against the six-hour pilot cap.

weeks.goal: Measure unprompted return within 14 days.
tasks: Run daily manual reviews and session-specific independent approval; send no reminders after session one.
Hold session two if safe; count original invitees who attended both sessions.
Apply the five-returner, €20, six-hour and documented-access gates; cancellation or unmet gates means failure.
Ask voluntary feedback on planning friction and streak pressure; do not label attendance as sponsor validation.

weeks.goal: Test payer interest and whether automation is justified.
tasks: If the pilot passes, show five shops the same hypothetical €20 weekly offer with aggregate reporting and clear sponsorship labelling.
Seek explicit conditional purchase commitments, not praise; record required outcomes and acquisition minutes.
Compare manual chat with a private scheduled-draft prototype using synthetic data only.
Inject stale permission, missing checker, duplicate trigger and ambiguous-delivery failures before considering live scheduling.

weeks.goal: Choose continue, simplify or stop.
tasks: Compare observed human minutes with the proposed economics; include recruitment and sponsor servicing.
Use mock cards to compare plain invitations with roulette and optional streaks; treat preference as exploratory, not causal retention evidence.
Keep manual tools unless scheduling removes measured work without bypassing approval.
Document failed gates, delete pilot identifiers on schedule, and propose a larger controlled test only if warranted.

economics.hypothesis: One sponsor at €20 per week could fund one neighbourhood group, but willingness to pay, renewals and sponsor outcomes are untested. Four paid weeks would hypothetically yield €80 gross; no payments are planned during the free attendance pilot.
economics.costAssumptions: Pilot cash cap €20; total organizer/checker effort cap six hours. Value labor at a hypothetical €12/hour. Assume €0 incremental software for the manual pilot, subject to tool checks. Workers paid-plan minimum is $5/month if chosen; budget FX separately. Payment fees, tax and insurance remain unpriced.
economics.unitEconomics: Target steady-state labor hypothesis: 60 minutes per sponsored week, costing €12 at the assumed rate. €20 revenue less €12 labor leaves €8 before software, acquisition, fees, tax, refunds and insurance. At two labor hours the contribution is already negative €4 before those costs.
unknowns: Inspection, travel, recruitment and sponsor acquisition time per group.
Whether any shop accepts €20 and what reporting it requires.
Payment method, fees, tax treatment and insurance needs before charging.
Cancellation policy: propose a full credit or refund for undelivered sponsored weeks; validate its cost.
Whether one sponsor can cover checking costs without unsafe shortcuts.

tests.hypothesis: At least five of ten invited students return without reminders.
tests.test: Human-run two-week free pilot with both times supplied at enrollment, two independently cleared circuits, consented attendance and a time/cash ledger.
tests.pass: At least five original invitees attend both weeks; all used stops have documented access approval; spend ≤€20 and effort ≤six hours.
tests.fail: Any gate missed, including cancellation or insufficient safe access. Record why rather than relaxing thresholds.

tests.hypothesis: Some local shops would conditionally buy the defined €20 weekly offer.
tests.test: After an attendance pass, a human presents the same offer to five shops, including labelled placement and consented aggregate reporting. Request a written conditional commitment; take no payment.
tests.pass: At least two shops explicitly accept €20 conditional on stated delivery terms; record acquisition time and remaining conditions.
tests.fail: Fewer than two commitments, or required outcomes cannot be delivered safely and privately. Commitments remain weaker than paid renewal.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed controls prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.
tests.test: Human-run tabletop replay: stale access, absent checker, duplicate trigger, failed preparation, uncertain send and withdrawal. Use synthetic records only.
tests.pass: Every unsafe case is blocked, no session is sent twice, retries stop at two, and s18 records each exception and resolution.
tests.fail: Any unapproved release, duplicate, exposed participant record or unowned exception; retain manual delivery and revise controls.

risks: A school-site announcement does not establish unrestricted access, opening hours or workout suitability.
Weather, injuries and changing equipment conditions require cancellation authority, not automated reassurance.
Friendship and novelty may explain return attendance; this small pilot cannot isolate roulette's effect.
Shared streaks can disclose routines or create pressure; keep participation optional and avoid individual rankings.
Human inspection and sponsor acquisition may overwhelm €20 weekly revenue.
Tool documentation and supplier prices establish neither successful operation nor customer demand.
unknowns: Who can grant access and what restrictions apply at each candidate stop?
Is competent independent exercise review available within the pilot limits?
Do participants prefer roulette to a plain invitation, and does it affect return behavior?
Which sponsor benefit is valuable without sharing participant identities?
Can weekly inspection and exception handling remain affordable without weakening checks?

plan.audience: Hypothesis: Riga SSE students organising weekend outings with friends. Start with ten students, one weekend and up to three operator-authorised craft sessions. Weekly value would be a fresh, verified shortlist, not a broad marketplace. No contact, tests, implementation or payments have occurred.
plan.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: operators pay 8% of attributable, completed booking value, excluding cancelled or refunded bookings. Seek written agreement before listing. Students would pay operators directly through their existing checkout; the founder would reconcile attendance and invoice commission afterward.
plan.valueProposition: Help a friend-group organiser compare a few suitable sessions by date, total price, location and available places, then reserve with the operator. Test against direct operator booking and self-organised discovery; convenience, repeat use and incremental operator sales remain unproven.
plan.firstTest: Proposed seven-day test: approach five operators and ten SSE students, spending under €30 and at most eight founder hours. Obtain permissions, cancellation terms and 8% fee agreement first. Pass only with two agreeing operators and three distinct students making genuine, operator-confirmed paid reservations without subsidy.
plan.mvp: Plan only: a manually maintained private session ledger, one read-only shortlist, an opt-in request form and operator-owned checkout links. Limit scope to three sessions for one weekend, then repeat only if gates pass. Store verification timestamps and referral IDs; confirm group capacity before redirecting. No app, accounts, scraping, pooled payments or recommendation model. Separate maker/checker approval gates publication; founder resolves stale stock, failed reservations and cancellations.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain written permission for session text, images, availability access and referral reconciliation; no scraping by default. Collect organiser email, party size and preferences, not friends' details or card data. Separate opt-in marketing from booking requests. Restrict ledger access; delete contact data after 30 days unless required for an active dispute or lawful records retention.

architecture.tool: Private ledger with a single designated writer
architecture.why: Use operator ID + session ID + start time as listing key. Assign one request ID per organiser/session; inspect existing pending or confirmed requests before sending another. Map operator booking IDs u

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga checklist: identify sessions expiring within 24 hours of their last verification, refresh authorised availability and review pending bookings. s03 checks by 10:00 whether the run occurred; otherwise all stale listings remain hidden.
loop.make: s30 would update draft matches using stated budget, party size and weekend preferences. Record source/version and timestamps; merge on listing key rather than append duplicates. Publish neither inferred availability nor unconfirmed group capacity.
loop.check: s14 would independently check operator evidence for date, timezone, total price, capacity and cancellation terms. Approval attaches to that exact version. Missing evidence, mismatch or age over 24 hours means suppression. Recheck capacity with the operator before a reservation handoff.
loop.deliver: s03 would publish approved listings and send only opted-in recipients a versioned shortlist. Log recipient, listing version and send status to prevent duplicate sends. Operators confirm paid booking IDs; after attendance, reconcile completion, refunds and the proposed commission. Review feedback weekly.
loop.exceptionOwner: s03, the fictional build/founder role, would own the queue. Retry failed reads at +15 and +60 minutes, then contact the operator manually. Never blindly retry payment or booking writes: reconcile first. Hide disputed listings, notify affected organisers within one working day and route refunds to operators; unresolved cases stay blocked.

weeks.goal: Test permission, willingness to pay and paid reservation interest before building.
tasks: s30 would approach five operators and ten SSE students; s03 would cap effort at eight hours and cash below €30.
Secure listing permission, checkout/referral arrangements, cancellation rules and proposed 8% completed-booking terms from two operators.
Run the first paid-reservation test manually; record refusals and abandoned steps. Stop if permissions or the reservation threshold fail.

weeks.goal: Specify and rehearse the smallest controlled workflow.
tasks: Create proposed ledger fields, state transitions and access rules; use synthetic records for rehearsals.
s14 would inject stale prices, sold-out sessions, duplicate requests and ambiguous booking outcomes; verify suppression and reconciliation.
Compare spreadsheet plus manual reminder with GitHub Actions and a custom Worker; keep the manual option unless measured effort warrants automation.

weeks.goal: If earlier gates pass, run one bounded, human-operated weekend pilot.
tasks: Offer no more than three verified sessions; run the daily maker/checker loop and log all exceptions and minutes.
Compare shortlist-assisted selection with direct discovery; count distinct paid reservations separately from completed attendance.
Ask operators to confirm booking attribution, attendance and refund status before calculating any commission.

weeks.goal: Test return behaviour and decide whether to continue.
tasks: Invite the original opt-in cohort to a second weekend shortlist without discounts; measure repeat requests and paid reservations.
Reconcile proposed commission against support time, acquisition effort, cancellations and collection costs.
Continue only if demand and workflow gates pass; otherwise narrow the offer, renegotiate pricing or stop. Document unresolved risks before any automation.

economics.hypothesis: Illustrative assumptions, not forecasts: €30 per participant booking and 8% commission imply €2.40 gross platform revenue per completed booking. Count each paid participant booking consistently; a group enquiry alone earns nothing.
economics.costAssumptions: Operator-owned checkout means operator processing costs, not platform costs, unless negotiated otherwise. Supplied Stripe pricing is 1.5% + €0.25 for standard EEA cards: €0.70 on hypothetical €30. Assume founder labour at €12/hour and 10 minutes per completed booking; hosting and acquisition need separate allocation.
economics.unitEconomics: At those assumptions, €2.40 commission minus €2 labour leaves €0.40 before acquisition, hosting, tax and collection. If the platform absorbed €0.70 processing, contribution would be -€0.30. A hypothetical €20 acquisition spend over three completions adds €6.67 each; three reservations do not establish viability.
unknowns: Actual session prices, average group size, attendance and refund rates.
Operator acceptance of commission, referral attribution and invoice collection.
Acquisition cost, repeat demand and human minutes per completed booking.
Payment-provider terms, taxes, currency conversion and any additional platform fees.

tests.hypothesis: Operators will authorise supply at 8%, and students will pay for the proposed offer.
tests.test: Human-run, seven-day outreach to five operators and ten students; offer only authorised sessions with explicit terms and operator checkout. No discounts or founder-funded reservations.
tests.pass: At least two operators agree in writing and three distinct students make operator-confirmed paid reservations; spend below €30 and effort at most eight hours.
tests.fail: Any threshold missed, or permission/payment evidence unavailable. Do not interpret interest or unpaid holds as paid reservations.

tests.hypothesis: The proposed control loop prevents stale listings and duplicate handoffs.
tests.test: s14 would run ten synthetic cases, including stale data, changed prices, sold-out capacity, repeated submissions, failed sends and ambiguous booking responses.
tests.pass: All unsafe cases suppressed; zero duplicate booking handoffs or sends; every unresolved case assigned to s03 with an audit trail.
tests.fail: Any unsafe publication, duplicate handoff, blind booking retry or unowned exception. Fix and rerun before a pilot.

tests.hypothesis: The shortlist reduces organiser effort and prompts a second-weekend action.
tests.test: Invite ten consenting students to counterbalanced shortlist and direct-discovery tasks; time selection. Offer a second weekend to the original cohort and record unsubsidised actions.
tests.pass: At least six finish both tasks, median shortlist time is 30% lower, and two original students make second-weekend paid reservations.
tests.fail: Any threshold missed; treat the sample as exploratory even if it passes, not proof of broad demand.

risks: Daily checks cannot guarantee live availability; require operator confirmation before checkout and never promise a place prematurely.
Friend-group coordination and cancellations may consume more labour than an 8% commission can support.
Operators may regard referrals as displaced direct sales or dispute attribution.
Small samples and novelty effects can exaggerate demand; paid reservations are not completed attendance or repeat economics.
Operator-managed payments reduce platform scope but do not remove privacy, consumer-information or dispute obligations.
unknowns: No supplied receipt establishes local craft demand, operator acceptance or willingness to pay.
Which operators permit reuse, availability access and referral reconciliation?
Can existing operator checkout handle group capacity and referral IDs without custom integration?
Will students return weekly rather than occasionally, and is curation better than direct discovery?
Research below supports scheduling capability and supplier costs only; it demonstrates neither customer demand nor a functioning product.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Workers official pricing
evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

lastWeeklyReview.milestone: Run one human-operated seven-day validation with five operator approaches, ten consenting students and at most three authorised sessions; cap total cash spending at €30 and all human effort at eight hours. Pass only if two operators provide written listing permission and 8% completed-booking terms, and three distinct students make unsubsidised, operator-confirmed paid reservations through operator checkout with traceable referral IDs. Fail if any
dissent: A concierge test need not already have scalable margins: coordinated group bookings could spread verification costs across several seats. That possibility justifies testing, but group size and labour savings remain hypotheses.

Seek written fee acceptance and measure

mentor.name: Sofia
mentor.lens: Product, engineering, autonomous operations and risk
mentor.experience: Invented 20-year product-builder and accelerator-adviser background; no real person or track record claimed.

plan.audience: Hypothesis: ten consenting adult friends from one Riga dorm, recruited by a human organizer through a permitted dorm channel. Preferred language, availability and accessibility needs must be established, not assumed.
plan.payerAndPrice: Proposed participant price: €0. No payer is validated. Defer sponsor outreach and payment integration until repeat participation and differentiation pass; any later sponsor price requires a separate test.
plan.valueProposition: Hypothesis: one weekly beginner-friendly outdoor card reduces planning effort versus arranging a walk. Include a 20-minute activity, meeting window, verified location, clear instructions and an equipment-free option. The city facility announcement establishes neither public access nor demand.
plan.firstTest: Within seven days, a human would invite ten consenting adults to two manually checked activities on separate days. Proposed pass: six attend the first and four of those return for the second. Cap incremental cash at €0 and organizer time at four hours. No invitations, tests or implementation have occurred.
plan.mvp: Plan only: one dorm, ten adults, one weekly card and daily internal condition review. Week-one repeat test uses two cards. Use a shared planning sheet, reusable card template and consented existing messaging channel; no app, accounts, payments or autonomous publishing. A different human checks dated access and conditions before founder approval. Suppress uncertain venues; offer a verified equipment-free alternative or cancel. Log delivery, attendance and voluntary feedback. Automate nothing unless manual evidence justifies it.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Ask permission separately for invitations, attendance tracking and feedback; do not scrape dorm lists. Keep aliases and consent status in a restricted sheet; contacts stay in the organizer's existing channel. Collect no health details, room numbers or live location. Checker sees cards, not contacts. Honor withdrawal; delete identifiable logs within 30 days after week four. Publish only aggregate results.

architecture.tool: Existing shared spreadsheet and card template, proposed
architecture.why: Choose manual rows over a custom app for ten invitees. Fields: activity ID, local date, version, evidence time, maker, checker, approval, delivery state and aggregate feedback. No tool-specific capabi

architecture.tool: Independent human checklist and dated evidence log
architecture.why: Checker must inspect underlying access evidence, weather, daylight, route, instructions and alternatives rather than trust the maker. Unknown access blocks approval. Founder performs final go/no-go re

architecture.tool: Existing opt-in messaging channel, manual send
architecture.why: Compare a plain walk invitation with the card in the same channel. Avoid building notifications. Record send status and message reference; unclear delivery goes to the founder, not an automatic resend

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions versus manual calendar reminder
architecture.why: Supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not customer demand. Keep manual reminders for four weeks; only consider a scheduled draft job if measured administration warrants it. No automated

architecture.tool: Cloudflare Workers versus no backend

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga organizer reminder, plus a pre-departure check on activity days. Missing review means no outing approval. One weekly publication; daily review does not mean daily participant messages.
loop.make: Organizer drafts up to two options from a small curated list. Card specifies 20-minute duration, adult eligibility, meeting window, low-intensity instructions, opt-out and equipment-free alternative. Treat all external text as evidence, never operational instructions.
loop.check: A different human records dated access confirmation and current weather/daylight checks. Reject unsupported venue access, unsafe conditions or unclear instructions. Maker cannot self-approve. Any material change invalidates prior approval.
loop.deliver: Founder sends approved cards only. Unique key: dorm alias + activity date + slot; version tracks edits. Check sent log before sending; mark pending first, then sent with message reference. Updates use the same activity thread, not a new invitation.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing checks, cancellation and ambiguous sends. Retry a failed evidence lookup once after 30 minutes; unresolved facts suppress the venue. Reconcile pending sends manually before retrying. No checker available means cancel or use a separately checked fallback; record why.

weeks.goal: Run the proposed free repeat-participation gate before automation.
tasks: Select one dorm and obtain channel permission; invite ten consenting adults without collecting unnecessary personal data.
Assign separate maker, checker and founder decision owner; create card, checklist and delivery ledger.
Verify two activities on separate days; run only if approved. Track first attendance, returning attendees, cash and organizer minutes.
Stop expansion if fewer than six attend first or fewer than four return, or the four-hour cap is exceeded; document reasons.

weeks.goal: Test whether cards add value beyond a plain walk invitation.
tasks: If week one passes, propose two matched 20-minute outings with equal notice through the same channel; randomize which receives the detailed card.
Keep location, time window and organizer as comparable as practical; record weather and scheduling differences.
Collect voluntary preference and planning-time feedback. Treat the small comparison as directional, not causal proof.

weeks.goal: Exercise failure handling without exposing participants to test hazards.
tasks: In an offline rehearsal, inject unknown access, stale weather evidence, unavailable checker and ambiguous delivery states.
Have the independent checker reject unsafe or unsupported drafts; confirm founder cancellation ownership.
Replay the same activity key twice and simulate a failed send; verify the ledger prevents a second invitation.
Continue at most one approved weekly card if earlier gates support it; log maker, checker and delivery minutes.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue manually, revise or stop.
tasks: Review repeat attendance, comparison feedback, blocked cards, duplicate attempts and total human time.
Estimate recurring cost using recorded minutes; do not infer sponsor willingness from free attendance.
Continue manual delivery only if usefulness and safe review appear repeatable; otherwise simplify to walks or stop.
Document any future automation requirement without deploying it; delete or anonymize records on the stated schedule.

economics.hypothesis: Free participation may justify a small manual wellbeing activity, not yet a business. Proposed four-week incremental cash budget is €0 using already available tools; sponsor revenue is untested and excluded.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

plan.audience: Hypothesis: foreign employees newly arrived in one Riga neighbourhood want short exploration quests and Latvian practice. Start with two consenting adults; cap any later pilot at five. Coworking staff are a proposed introduction channel. Team IDs describe fictional roles.

plan.valueProposition: Proposed value: one independently checked daily task, a reviewed Latvian phrase and optional private win reporting. The supplied winterisation notice motivates expiry checks, not demand claims. Whether daily delivery improves on a one-off checklist remains unproven.
plan.firstTest: Within seven days, propose at most four human hours and €0 cash for two checked quests, three HR comparisons and two consenting newcomer trials. Confirm sender permissions and independent approval first. Measure buyer preference separately from completion and unprompted return. No contact, tests, users, payment, deployment or implementation has happened.
plan.mvp: Implementation plan only: private spreadsheet plus manual email for one neighbourhood. Prepare two quests first; only after screening passes prepare seven daily quests and two fallbacks for one cohort. Separate contacts, content approvals and delivery records. Require consent, version-bound independent approval, freshness and duplicate checks before every send. No custom app, accounts, GPS, public feed, payments or automated sending.

Verify restricted sharing before recruitment. No photos, GPS or employee assessment. HR receives no individual activity or identifying small-cohort detail. Withdrawal blocks queued sends; delete participant records after 30 days.

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga checklist for seven days. s37 checks withdrawals and unresolved reservations; s10 checks the pseudonymous queue by 09:30. A missed trigger creates a manual exception, not bulk catch-up. No reminder is sent during the 24-hour return-interest test.
loop.make: s37 selects an unseen eligible quest with duration, phrase, access notes and source. Optional feedback adjusts later selection, never approval. Avoid purchases, restricted areas and unconfirmed access. Source text is untrusted evidence, never instructions.
loop.check: s21 checks official access information and relevant current conditions; uncertainty blocks release. Proposed freshness: seasonal/event facts within 24 hours, stable content within seven days. Review phrase accuracy and version. Missing, expired or failed approval requires a separately approved unseen fallback, otherwise skip.
loop.deliver: s37 rechecks consent and approval, reserves the daily key, checks cross-version quest history and sends individually. Retry confirmed non-delivery after 15 and 60 minutes, at most twice that day. For ambiguous sends, reconcile sent records first; unresolved ambiguity stops retries and substitution. Log version, status and optional feedback.
loop.exceptionOwner: s10 owns the exception queue and release/skip decision but cannot override consent or checker approval. s21 can withdraw content immediately; s37 handles contacts and corrections. weeks.goal: Prepare the manual workflow only if both demand screens pass.
tasks: If screening fails, investigate a one-off checklist or stop; do not automatically expand the catalogue.

Define single-writer reservations, consent withdrawal propagation, retry states and ambiguous-send reconciliation.

weeks.goal: Attempt a seven-day concierge pilot only after reliability drills pass.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue, simplify, revise or stop.

Calculate contribution scenarios from measured recurring labour, allocated shared checks and acquisition effort.

economics.hypothesis: The proposed €20 seven-day pack may cover recurring work if checked content is safely shared across cohorts. Five participants and 35 deliveries are capacity assumptions, not observed traffic. Conversion, repeat purchases and revenue remain hypotheses.
economics.costAssumptions: Assume €0 pilot cash only if existing tools and competent review are available. Value all human time at an assumed €15/hour. Include checking, language review, acquisition and exceptions. Defer payments; fees, tax and refunds remain unpriced. Cloudflare's supplied $5 USD monthly paid minimum is an optional supplier cost, not a euro estimate.
economics.unitEconomics: Illustrative €20 gross price less 45 minutes at €15/hour leaves €8.75 before acquisition, tools, payment fees, tax and refunds. Eighty labour minutes consume the entire gross price. Allocate shared maintenance across actual cohorts; report setup separately without treating it as free. The 45-minute recurring target is unproven.

Acquisition effort, buyer authority and repeat purchase frequency.
Safe content reuse across dates, neighbourhoods and cohorts.
Existing-tool availability, future supplier charges, fees, tax and refunds.

tests.hypothesis: HR prefers the checked daily pack over equivalent municipal links and a static checklist at €20.
tests.test: Human presents both formats to three confirmed HR budget owners in varied order. Keep content scope comparable; ask preference, specific reason and nonbinding willingness to buy the seven-day pack. Take no payment.
tests.pass: At least one prefers the daily pack and records willingness to buy at €20 with a specific reason. Treat this only as a screening signal.
tests.fail: Zero qualifying buyers fails the screen. Fewer than three comparisons is inconclusive and blocks expansion.

tests.hypothesis: Newcomers complete a checked quest and voluntarily seek another.
tests.test: Two consenting adults receive a checked quest and a clear way to request another. Send no reminder for 24 hours. Afterwards ask how the format compares with the equivalent checklist.
tests.pass: Both report completing one quest and at least one independently requests another within 24 hours. Record comparative usefulness separately.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed. Distinguish access failure from lack of interest; consider a one-off pack if daily return fails.

tests.hypothesis: Manual controls prevent invalid or duplicate releases within a plausible recurring labour budget.
tests.test: Human rehearses expired approval, edited content, failed access, withdrawn consent, duplicate trigger, confirmed send failure and ambiguous send. Time a simulated seven-day workflow with allocated independent checking.
tests.pass: All seven scenarios block, substitute or reconcile correctly; no duplicate or blind ambiguous retry occurs. Projected recurring labour is at most 45 minutes per cohort, with setup reported separately.
tests.fail: Any invalid, withdrawn-consent or duplicate send, uncontrolled retry, or labour above target requires revision before expansion.

risks: The dated winterisation notice supports freshness controls, not current access, safe routes or customer demand.
Independent checking, language review and acquisition may exceed the proposed price's labour allowance.
Nonbinding HR intent may not become a purchase; participant return does not establish employer value.
Optional wins may expose identity or location; keep collection private, minimal and separate from HR reporting.
Manual duplicate prevention depends on one sender and disciplined reservation reconciliation.
Useful shared content may lower later costs, but reuse must not bypass freshness checks.
unknowns: No actual customer contact, tests, users, payment, deployment or implementation has happened.
Newcomer needs, reachable HR buyers and incremental value over a checklist remain unverified.
Reviewer competence, availability and current quest-access evidence require confirmation.
Permissions, failure controls, labour allocations and deletion procedures remain untested.

There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

learning.title: Separate supplier arithmetic from buyer evidence
learning.text: For this proposed €20 pack, the supplied standard EEA card rate would imply €0.55 processing cost, leaving €19.45 before labour and other costs. That calculation can bound a labour hypothesis, but cannot establish willingness to pay. Test the HR preference against a static checklist before adding payment infrastructure.

sparring.question: Should the first buyer test prioritise a one-off checked welcome pack or a daily quest service, given that the supplied evidence supports changing local information but not daily engagement?
sparring.answer: Prioritise the one-off checked welcome pack as the first buyer hypothesis, not as a validated business. R63c54b9e23dc supports information becoming outdated; it establishes neither demand for checked packs nor daily engagement. Your proposed tomorrow-return measure tests newcomer behaviour, not whether HR will buy. Run one discriminating buyer test: show six prospective HR budget holders two equally specific offers—two neighbourhood-specific checked quests delivered once for €20 per cohort of up to five, versus one checked quest daily for seven days at the same introductory cohort price. Allow 'neither'; request a written purchase commitment

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

tests.hypothesis: At least four of ten commuters voluntarily return for a distinct episode.

tests.pass: At least four of ten confirm playing two distinct episodes within their windows; recruitment and publication finish within €20 and six total team hours.

tests.hypothesis: Manual controls prevent unsafe and duplicate releases at manageable effort.
tests.test: Founder and separate checker rehearse five dummy failures: duplicate event, stale date, unclear rights, failed upload and uncertain send. Also time three clean episode rehearsals. No drill content reaches volunteers.
tests.pass: All unsafe cases held, no duplicate authorized, bounded retries logged and every exception owned; clean rehearsals average at most 60 team minutes each.
tests.fail: Any unsafe approval, duplicate authorization, unowned exception or production average above 60 minutes. Fix and repeat before expanding.

risks: Ten convenience-sample volunteers may report novelty or politeness rather than durable value.
Optional reports can undercount listening; social pressure can inflate positive reports. Do not compensate with covert tracking.
A dated cultural invitation does not establish daily source supply, reuse permission or present availability.
Independent checking and rights review may exceed the time cap; skip rather than fabricate or self-approve.
Weekend places may be cancelled or inaccessible; verify details and avoid availability guarantees.
Free listening cannot establish a sustainable payer; sponsorship could compromise editorial independence.
unknowns: No customer contact, tests, users, payment, deployment or implementation has happened.
Language, channel, accessibility needs and recruitment feasibility remain untested.
Source permissions, service privacy controls and editorial workload require human verification.
No supplied receipt demonstrates commuter demand, sustained listening or willingness to pay.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.
